lessons.title: Residential Returns: Low Yields, Appreciation Bets and Emotional Pricing

children.text: Every family WhatsApp group has an uncle who says, "I bought my flat for ₹60 lakh and today it is worth ₹1.2 crore. Property never fails." Doubling in ten years sounds spectacular. It works out to 7.2% a year, before stamp duty, interiors, brokerage, maintenance and the interest on the loan. This lesson shows you how residential returns are really built in India: a thin layer of rent, a large bet on appreciation, and prices that are often set by emotion rather than income.

body.text: In Indian residential property, rent barely pays the running costs. Almost all of your return is a bet that someone will pay much more for the flat later.

children.text: From Gross Yield to Net Yield

Take a ready 2BHK on Sarjapur Road, Bengaluru, bought for ₹1 crore and rented at ₹28,000 a month. The gross yield is ₹3.36 lakh ÷ ₹1 crore = 3.36%. That is the number brokers quote. Now subtract what the owner actually pays.

body.caption: Sarjapur Road 2BHK: annual rent to net income

cells: ₹4,000 a month, often paid by the owner

markDefs.definition: Property price divided by annual rent. It shows how many years of rent it would take to pay for the property. Higher numbers mean rent is small relative to price.

children.text: A 3.36% headline becomes 2.28% in your hands, and that is before tax and before the roughly 6% to 8% you paid in stamp duty and registration to buy the flat. The
price-to-rent ratio
makes the point bluntly: ₹1 crore ÷ ₹3.36 lakh = about 30. At today's rent, it takes 30 years of gross rent just to equal the purchase price.

stats.label: Price-to-rent ratio
stats.context: Years of rent to equal the price

stats.label: EMI vs rent
stats.context: On an 80% loan at 8% for 20 years

children.text: Why Residential Is Really an Appreciation Bet

body.latex: \text{Total Return} \approx \text{Net Rental Yield} + \text{Annual Price Appreciation} - \text{Transaction Cost Drag}
body.caption: A rough rule. Transaction costs such as stamp duty and brokerage reduce annual returns most when the holding period is short.

children.text: With a net yield near 2%, appreciation has to do nearly all the work. Here is the same Sarjapur flat held for 10 years under three appreciation scenarios. We assume ₹7 lakh of stamp duty and registration on entry (so ₹1.07 crore invested), 2% brokerage on exit, and net rent of ₹2.28 lakh a year kept as cash, not reinvested.

body.title: Annual return on the Sarjapur flat by price growth scenario (%)
Show me the math: the 5% scenario

children.text: Sale price after 10 years: ₹1 crore × 1.05¹⁰ = ₹1.629 crore. After 2% brokerage: ₹1.629 crore × 0.98 = ₹1.596 crore.
Add 10 years of net rent at ₹2.28 lakh: ₹22.8 lakh. Total wealth: ₹1.596 crore + ₹0.228 crore = ₹1.824 crore.
Annual return: (₹1.824 crore ÷ ₹1.07 crore)^(1/10) minus 1 = 1.705^0.1 minus 1 = 5.5% a year.

Two simplifications cut in opposite directions. Rent in real life usually rises each year, which helps. Rent kept as cash rather than reinvested earns nothing, which hurts. Treat the results as a fair rough guide, not a precise forecast.

The pattern is clear. Your return lands close to the price growth rate plus a small top-up from rent. If prices grow at 5%, you earn about 5.5%. So the only question that really matters for a residential investment is how fast this particular flat's price will grow, and how sure you are about that.
The Monthly Gap When You Borrow

markDefs.definition: When the income from an asset, such as rent, is lower than the cost of holding it, such as loan EMIs and maintenance, so the owner must top up the difference every month.

children.text: Most Indians buy with a home loan, which makes the thin yield bite harder. Borrow ₹80 lakh at 8% for 20 years and the EMI is about ₹66,915 a month. The tenant pays ₹28,000. You fund the remaining ₹38,915 every month, plus maintenance and property tax, from your salary. That shortfall is called
negative carry

body.text: Leverage magnifies the appreciation bet in both directions. If prices rise strongly, the loan boosts your return on the down payment. If prices stall for five years, as they did in several Delhi NCR and Mumbai suburbs through the second half of the 2010s, you pay the monthly gap for years with little to show for it.

children.text: Emotional Pricing: Why Flats Ignore Rent

If investors set flat prices, prices would track rent the way office values do. They do not, because most residential buyers are end users. A family buying its first home is paying for security, status, a school catchment and the pride of ownership, often with help from parents. It does not care that the yield is 2.5%. Investors who buy alongside them pay the same emotional price without getting the emotional benefit.

columns.label: End-user buyer asks
points: Is it near the office and a good school?
Will our family feel safe and settled here?
Is this a good time to stop paying rent?

columns.label: Investor should ask
points: What is the net yield after all costs?
What price growth do I need to beat my alternatives?
How long could the flat sit vacant?
Who will buy it from me, and at what price?
What is my real return after inflation?

body.text: Residential prices in India rarely fall sharply in rupee terms. Sellers who do not need cash simply wait rather than cut. Weak markets usually show up as a "time correction": prices flat for years while inflation quietly erodes their real value. That is less painful to look at, but it can be just as costly.

children.text: Nominal vs Real Appreciation

A flat that rises 5% a year while consumer inflation runs at 5% has not made you richer. It has only kept pace. Always ask what the appreciation looks like after inflation, and compare it with what the same money could earn in other assets over the same period. For a data-based view of how prices have actually moved in different cities, the RBI publishes a quarterly House Price Index.

body.label: RBI Database on Indian Economy (DBIE)
body.description: Search for the House Price Index to see how residential prices have moved across major Indian cities over time, instead of relying on developer or broker claims.

body.title: Calculate: Net Yield on a Kondapur Flat
body.prompt: A flat in Kondapur, Hyderabad costs ₹90 lakh and rents for ₹27,000 a month. Annual costs are ₹42,000 maintenance, ₹10,000 property tax, one month of vacancy and ₹15,000 for repairs and brokerage. What is the net yield, to two decimal places?

body.title: Quick Check: What Drives the Return?
body.question: A residential flat has a net yield of 2%. Over a 10-year holding period, which factor will most influence the investor's total return?
options: Whether the tenant pays by UPI or cheque
The rate at which the flat's price grows
Whether the rent agreement is renewed every 11 or 12 months
body.explanation: With only about 2% coming from rent, price growth drives most of the return. A difference of 3 percentage points in annual appreciation changes the outcome far more than anything happening on the rent side.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Years of Rent
body.textWithBlank: Dividing a property's price by its annual rent gives the price-to-___ ratio.
body.explanation: The price-to-rent ratio shows how many years of rent it takes to equal the price. A ratio near 30, common for Indian big-city flats, signals a yield of roughly 3%.

body.title: Scenario: "My Flat Doubled"
body.scenario: Arjun bought a flat in Thane in 2015 for ₹60 lakh. He paid about ₹4 lakh in stamp duty and registration and spent ₹5 lakh on interiors. He has lived in it since. In 2025 he sold it for ₹1.2 crore, paying 1% brokerage. He tells everyone he doubled his money and that property beat every other investment.
body.prompt: What was his actual annual return on the money he put in, and what is his claim missing?
body.modelAnswer: His all-in cost was ₹60 lakh + ₹4 lakh + ₹5 lakh = ₹69 lakh. His net sale proceeds were ₹1.2 crore × 0.99 = ₹1.188 crore. His annual return is (₹1.188 crore ÷ ₹69 lakh)^(1/10) minus 1 = about 5.6%, not the 7.2% that "doubling in ten years" implies. His claim also ignores 10 years of society maintenance and property tax, and any home loan interest he paid. In his favour, he lived rent-free, and the rent he saved is a real economic benefit worth adding. The honest comparison is his total picture against what the same ₹69 lakh and the same monthly outgo would have grown to in other assets.

cards.definition: Annual rent minus maintenance, property tax, vacancy and repairs, divided by the property price.
Property price divided by annual rent; around 30 for many Indian big-city flats.
When rent is lower than the EMI and holding costs, so the owner tops up the gap every month.
A market where prices stay flat for years instead of falling, so real value declines through inflation.
Prices set by end users paying for security, status and lifestyle rather than by the rent a property earns.
Price growth after subtracting inflation; the increase in actual purchasing power.

points: A 3% to 3.5% gross yield on an Indian big-city flat often shrinks to around 2% to 2.5% after maintenance, property tax, vacancy and repairs.
Price-to-rent ratios near 30 mean rent is tiny relative to price, so residential returns are mostly an appreciation bet.
Your long-run return lands close to the flat's annual price growth plus a small top-up from rent, minus transaction costs.
With a home loan, EMIs can be more than twice the rent, creating a monthly gap you fund from income.
End users set residential prices based on emotion and affordability, not yield, so investors pay the same emotional premium.
Always check appreciation after inflation, and check claims like "my flat doubled" against the full cost of owning it.

body.text: All prices, rents, costs, loan rates and growth scenarios in this lesson are illustrative assumptions, not forecasts. Stamp duty and registration charges vary by state. This lesson is educational and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any property.
